### Related literature {#sec-literature}

This paper sits at the intersection of real options, strategic investment, structural credit risk, and the economics of AI. I take the four building blocks in turn (real options and capacity choice, strategic investment and R&D races, structural credit risk, and the economics of AI) and then state the marginal contribution.

The real-options foundation rests on @mcdonald1986value for optimal timing of irreversible investment and @pindyck1988irreversible for capacity choice.^[Other foundational contributions include @brennan1985evaluating and @bernanke1983irreversibility.] @guo2005investment model demand with regime-dependent drift and volatility, showing large investment jumps upon favorable regime arrival; @decamps2006irreversible study irreversible investment with alternative projects under regime switching, using a two-regime structure with an absorbing state that is close to the present paper's $L \to H$ transition. The key difference is that their framework does not include strategic interaction, training-inference allocation, or default risk. The capacity-choice side of the problem is also the subject of a large operations management literature, surveyed by @vanmieghem2003capacity, which studies how much capacity to install under demand uncertainty and how flexible that capacity should be. The closest construct there is resource flexibility: @chod2005resource show that a flexible resource allocated across products *after* demand is observed substitutes for capacity and interacts with pricing. Compute is flexible in exactly this sense, since the same GPU cluster can train or serve. The allocation studied here, however, is a commitment made at installation, and its training component pays off only in a different demand regime. It is also priced jointly with the firm's default decision rather than treated as an operational problem for a solvent firm.

Strategic real-options models replace the single decision maker with rivals whose entry erodes the option value of waiting [@grenadier2002option].^[See also @weeds2002strategic on R\&D delay and @fudenberg1985preemption for game-theoretic foundations.] The closest strategic-investment paper is @huisman2015strategic, who study a duopoly with joint timing and capacity choice. I extend their framework with endogenous default risk, training-inference allocation, diminishing returns, and regime switching.

@aguerrevere2003equilibrium studies equilibrium incremental capacity investment in oligopoly with time-to-build and the option to idle capacity, showing that operating flexibility can make firms *expand* in response to greater uncertainty. @aguerrevere2009real draws out the asset-pricing implication that installed capacity and competitive intensity jointly determine the composition of firm value between assets in place and growth options, and hence expected returns. That mapping from capacity to risk exposure is the antecedent of the training-beta conjecture of @sec-discussion, under which firms with larger training fractions carry higher equity betas, with the difference that here the risk composition shifts with the *split* of a given capacity rather than with its level.

@lambrecht2003real study real options in duopoly with incomplete information, where firms have private signals about the investment payoff. Their setting is related to the present paper's heterogeneous beliefs about the AGI arrival rate $\lambda$, the Poisson intensity of the switch to regime $H$ formalized in @sec-model, but they do not model the training-inference allocation or the endogenous default mechanism that links beliefs to survival. The present paper's emphasis on heterogeneous beliefs about $\lambda$ as a driver of cross-sectional variation connects to the broader literature on disagreement and speculation [@harrison1978speculative; @scheinkman2003overconfidence], though here disagreement operates through comparative statics in $\lambda$ rather than through equilibrium trading under heterogeneous priors. @grenadier2011real develop real options signaling games in which investment timing conveys private information, which bears on the dynamic belief updating about $\lambda$ raised as a future direction in @sec-conclusion. @bouis2009multistage provide an $N$-firm sequential entry framework that could extend the duopoly analysis.

The investment dynamics in this paper also connect to the literature on patent races and R&D competition. @loury1979market models firms choosing R&D intensity to accelerate a stochastic Poisson breakthrough, showing that competition leads to socially excessive duplication of effort. @reinganum1982strategic extends the framework to asymmetric firms, demonstrating that the frontrunner invests more aggressively. The parallel with the leader's earlier entry in the preemption equilibrium of Proposition 3 is loose: Reinganum's frontrunner is defined by its technological position, whereas here the leader's role is itself an outcome of the timing game. @harris1987racing model R&D as a race with position-dependent investment incentives, producing a "discouragement effect" for lagging firms that echoes the follower's delayed entry in the duopoly equilibrium; in the present model the *allocation* margin is immune to this discouragement (Proposition 3(ii)), so position affects when firms invest, not how they split capacity. @grossman1986optimal study simultaneous timing and scale choices in R&D competition under uncertainty, combining elements of the capacity and timing decisions modeled here. The key departure from this literature is the dual role of capacity: in standard R&D races, investment during the race is pure cost with no concurrent revenue, whereas here, installed capacity generates inference revenue before AGI arrives and training quality determines competitive position afterwards, creating the allocation trade-off that is absent from existing race models.

The firm's default decision follows the structural credit-risk tradition of @merton1974pricing and @leland1994corporate.^[@blackcox1976valuing extend to a first-passage setting.] A well-developed branch of this literature already embeds regime switching in the Leland framework. @hackbarth2006capital let cash flows depend on a two-state macroeconomic regime and derive default and financing policies that adapt to the cycle, reproducing countercyclical leverage ratios and strictly positive short-maturity credit spreads; @chen2010macroeconomic and @bhamra2010levered add a consumption-based pricing kernel, so that risk prices, leverage, and regime-contingent default boundaries are determined jointly. Proposition 2 is therefore not the first default boundary derived in a regime-switching environment; those papers in fact solve the fully coupled system with regime-contingent boundaries, whereas @eq-default-boundary uses a single boundary that embeds the switch in unconditional expectation (@sec-model documents the resulting approximation error).

The regime-switching credit literature makes the default boundary depend on the state; the present model makes it depend on how the firm has positioned itself for the state it is waiting for. In those models the regime governs the cash-flow process exogenously, so the size of the growth option is not a decision variable and cannot be traded off against current cash flow. Here the firm chooses $\phi$, and that choice determines both the regime-$H$ continuation value and the regime-$L$ coupon coverage, which is why the default boundary can be *decreasing* in the training fraction (@eq-phi-underbar).

The most closely related papers combining investment and default are @hackbarth2014capital (real options with endogenous default and product market competition) and @kumar2018optimal (joint leverage and irreversible capacity choice, showing they are substitutes).^[@sundaresan2015dynamic model growth options with default risk; @bolton2019investment model financial constraints on investment.] The present model integrates endogenous default into the strategic capacity-choice game, building on @hackbarth2012corporate for the investment-financing framework. The Leland default framework is most natural for public-debt issuers; for the VC-backed archetypes in the calibration, "default" should be interpreted broadly as financial distress (failed funding round, liquidity crisis), consistent with @gornall2020squaring on the gap between VC valuations and the underlying economics of startup financing.

The model's technology assumptions come from the economics of AI. AI training exhibits power-law scaling [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training], motivating the concave production function; @jones1995rdbased and @bloom2020ideas study diminishing returns in idea production. @agrawal2019economics frame AI as a prediction technology and connect inference demand to economic value creation. On the training-inference allocation, the closest analog is @akcigit2018growth on exploitation versus exploration R\&D, set in a multi-product firm rather than in a compute allocation problem.^[@berk1999optimal develop growth option decompositions that motivate the scale-gap diagnostic of @sec-valuation and Internet Appendix G, which is a comparative-statics normalization rather than a growth-option decomposition. @babina2024artificial and @eisfeldt2023generative provide empirical context on AI investment and valuations; these papers could in principle discipline certain calibration inputs (e.g., AI firm betas, investment intensities), though the rapidly evolving nature of the sector limits the stability of such inputs.]

On the macroeconomics of AI, @aghion2019artificial, @acemoglu2024simple, @korinek2024scenarios, and @jones2024agi analyze the growth implications of transformative AI in general equilibrium. The Baumol mechanism in @aghion2019artificial, under which growth is limited by the tasks that remain essential and hard to automate, plays a role loosely analogous to the diminishing returns $\alpha < 1$ imposed at the firm level here. The present paper is partial equilibrium (it takes the demand process and the discount rate as given) and therefore complements these general equilibrium analyses by providing a micro-founded model of the firm-level investment and allocation decisions that aggregate into the industry dynamics those papers study.^[@novymarx2007operating shows that operating leverage amplifies systematic risk, relevant to the operating cost parameter $\delta$.]

The marginal contribution is the combination of these building blocks around a single margin, the *training-inference allocation under regime-specific competition with endogenous default*. Each block above exists in isolation; what is new is the firm's choice of how to split capacity between current revenue generation and future capability building, where (a) the relevant competitive variable switches across regimes (inference capacity today, training quality tomorrow), (b) the allocation determines competitive position differently across regimes, and (c) the allocation affects firm survival through the continuation-value channel in the default boundary.

Two of the paper's results turn on this mechanism: a *faith-based survival* condition (@eq-phi-underbar) in which training investment lowers the default boundary by raising the expected post-AGI continuation value, and an asymmetric *Dario's dilemma* in which the training channel makes conservative underinvestment costlier in expected value than aggressive overinvestment of the same magnitude, while leverage concentrates the tail (default) risk on the aggressive side. Each adjacent literature is missing one of the ingredients that make this mechanism operative. The models that combine capacity choice with endogenous default [@hackbarth2014capital; @kumar2018optimal] treat installed capital as homogeneous, so there is no split to choose. The regime-switching credit models [@hackbarth2006capital; @chen2010macroeconomic; @bhamra2010levered] take the cash-flow process, and with it the size of the growth option, as exogenous, so the firm cannot buy survival by sacrificing current revenue. The allocation problems closest in structure [@akcigit2018growth; @chod2005resource] are solved for firms whose survival is not at stake. The contribution is the joint presence of the three, not any one of them.
